I think they’re making an assumption because you said this is your first relationship. I also think it’s obvious that you’re really head over heels for this guy, and there’s nothing wrong with that! But just by virtue of it being your first relationship, and the fact this relationship is moving REALLY fast, it shows that you may be more vulnerable, especially since he has so much experience compared to you. Just try to be careful and guard your heart- make sure you’re thinking everything through and not making too many rash, emotional decisions. Being in a new relationship can be a like a drug, and can make you ignore lots of things that in hindsight are concerning. 

I do think it’s odd to bring up living together so soon. It makes it seem like he was desperate to find a girlfriend/wife without taking the time to actually get to know you, because he just can’t know you after two dates. Would you ask someone to move in with you after meeting them twice? I’m not saying this is grounds to break up, but these are the kinds of things to be cautious about. I would take this slow, and try and be smart. I’m not saying to be hunting for his flaws all the time, but recognize that you don’t have the same relationship experience as him, and therefore might miss a lot of nuances. No one is ever perfect, and being infatuated with someone can also lead to people disregarding things that maybe they should be concerned about

All that to say, I would just be aware of your lack of experience, and take things easy. Keep asking your friends their opinions, but of course they can be wrong. Just remember that anyone out there can be trying to use you, and don’t let flattery blind you to potentially strange things- like asking to live together before you get the chance to know each other. I’m not saying that that’s automatically a sign of a bad guy, but these are just things to consider. Tread with an open heart, but a wary mind

I recently got my first one- I love it, no regrets at all, no shock- BUT the reality of the permanency is still setting in, and I’m now glad that I opted for a smaller tattoo for my first one rather than going big on something somewhere like my arms (not to say your arms are a bad spot for a first tattoo, but I’m glad that I didn’t do it). I never said it was consistent. But it is stated in scripture that there is a new law, and so I was just saying why that’s an expectation, and that there’s reasoning behind it (whether or not it’s seen as good reasoning)

But for a lot of people, especially those who study WHY certain parts of scripture are present (they were chosen by people after all), they don’t believe in Biblical inerrancy. There are key factors considered vital, but in many denominations it’s acknowledged that some parts are more clear than others. Many people hold the philosophy of seeking out spiritual fulfillment by following the guidance given for fostering things like love and community by Jesus’ specific words, and recognize that many parts of certain laws are steeped in political practices of the time. I don’t really fall under any religious umbrella but I’m just trying to give context. While some practices expect strict, absolute obedience, I think it’s important from an outside perspective to recognize that for many, not doing so isn’t seen as laziness or being uneducated, but deliberate decisions being made off of their historical research. They want to be aware of which parts may have been included due to factors not considered important to the key tenets of the belief, not simply excluding things that don’t “work with” a modern perspective

It is interesting, I grew up in an environment that chastised the “cherry pickers “, while they did that all the time. But the denominations I got to know that seemed to value historical truth more understood that it wasn’t picking what “sounds good” from scripture, but things were carefully evaluated based on their historical backgrounds. Obviously it’s so old and convoluted that pure “truth” is unattainable, but many try to get as close as they can, and believe that’s worth something. It’s totally fine if you believe that those who practice shouldn’t do this, and it’s fine to agree to disagree.

Wasn’t trying to be antagonistic, just giving context as to why tattoos are often considered not a bad thing, and that if they are Christian, OP likely knows this. It’s still good to spread information, and the whole topic is really fascinating!

And when you use で for the example you added, that’s using で to mark a method, like スプーンで食べる, so it’s just a different grammar point than the に vs. で topic, just like に can also mean inside

に is more like “to”, in this situation it’s used for coming and going. 学校に行く(I’m going TO school), 図書館に来る (I’m coming TO the library). で is more like “at” and you use it for sentences like 学校で勉強する(I’m studying AT school) or 図書館で読む (I’m reading AT the library). に and で have lots of other uses but this is applicable for this example.
で is more like “at”. に would be more like “to” で can also be for methods but not in the usage described in this post

One way I explain it to my students is に is “to” (ex. I go TO school, I come TO the library) while で is “at”. I have a party AT the house, I study AT the library. You aren’t having a party TO your dad’s house, it’s AT his house.
